newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean union calls for biggest ever strike.
newsitem.headline: South Korean union calls for biggest ever strike.

text.p: South Korea's main labour union group called on Thursday for the biggest strike in the nation's history, while prosecutors threatened to send police to seize militant unionists holed up at a Seoul cathedral.
Thousands of workers turned central Seoul into a rubble-strewn battleground as they clashed with riot police, sending terrified shoppers racing for cover.

The Federation of Korean Trade Unions, which claims 1.2 million members, said a two-day strike would begin on Tuesday to try to force the government to dump a new labour law that allows companies to lay off workers.
Power, port and railway workers were urged to go on partial strike and all others to join a full stoppage.
"The federation calls on all its members to join the largest strike ever, led especially by the public sector," president Park In-sang told a news conference.
City buses and subways would stop and hospitals, banks, hotels, taxis and state industries, including the tobacco monopoly, would be affected.
State prosecutors issued warrants for seven leaders of the more militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions to appear in court on Friday.
Several hundred riot police burst into confederation headquarters and offices of its hospital and auto-union affiliates late on Thursday to seize documents, a union official said.

Confederation president Kwon Young-kil and his lieutenants said they would refuse to comply with the order to appear in court. They are huddled in a plastic tent in the grounds of Myongdong Cathedral guarded by car workers with iron bars.
"If they don't appear tomorrow morning we will have to send a large number of police officers to execute the warrants," a prosecution official said.

Any attempt to storm the church grounds would almost certainly spark fierce clashes and reignite strikes that began to fizzle on Thursday as workers streamed back to shipyards and car plants in response to government threats.

Earlier, a global trade union group, the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, appealed to the International Labour Organisation to intervene immediately to prevent arrests of the seven labour leaders.
On Wednesday the South Korean ministers of interior, justice and labour threatened "stern measures" against strikes that have been declared illegal.

By Thursday strikes had almost completely crumbled at shipyards, and unions at giant Hyundai Group in Ulsan -- a hotbed of union militancy -- had retreated from all-out stoppages and begun "partial strikes".
It appeared that unions were now adopting disruption tactics to avoid the threat of legal action against unlawful strikes.
Unions claimed 190,000 workers were on strike, but that number included unionists on work-to-rule. The labour ministry put the figure at about 75,000.
The country's previous biggest industrial action was in 1989 when the government said some 400,000 workers downed tools. But those strikes dragged on for months.

Around 4,000 workers ripped up paving stones around Myongdong and hurled them at squads riot officers who fired back choking tear gas that caught shoppers and office workers heading home during the evening rush hour.
It was some of the worst violence since the strikes erupted on December 26 after the law was rammed through parliament.
Kwon, whose outlawed confederation claims half a million members, called for international pressure on the South Korean government to repeal the new labour law.
The International Confederation of Free Trade Unions condemned the legislation that it said added to existing violations of union rights.

These included provision for replacing strikers "as temporarily employed strike breakers", for dismissed workers to lose the right to belong to a union, and for a ban on companies paying strikers during a stoppage.
South Korean opposition parties jointly challenged the law in the Seoul constitutional court and appealed to the court to suspend the bill until a ruling is made.

President Kim Young-sam and senior government and ruling party officials have all made clear they will not retreat from legislation they say is needed to make the labour market more flexible, cut industrial costs and shore up the country's sagging competitiveness.
